quizzes.topic: Parallel Forces and Moment of Force (Torque)

questions.q: The line along which a force acts is called the:
options: line of action of the force
questions.explanation: The line of action may be extended to find the moment arm.

questions.q: Parallel forces acting in the same direction are called:
questions.explanation: E.g. pushing a cart with both hands.

questions.q: Parallel forces acting in opposite directions are called:
questions.explanation: E.g. turning a bike handle with both hands.

questions.q: The turning effect produced in a body about a fixed point due to applied force is called:
questions.explanation: Torque causes change in rotational motion.

questions.q: The SI unit of moment of force is:
questions.explanation: τ = F × d → newton × metre.

questions.q: Moment of force τ is given by:
options: F × d (d = perpendicular distance from axis to line of action)
questions.explanation: The perpendicular distance d is called the moment arm.

questions.q: A force of 60 N acts at a moment arm of 0.40 m. The torque is:
questions.explanation: τ = 60 × 0.40 = 24 N m (book Example 4.1).

questions.q: When the line of action of a force passes through the axis of rotation, the torque is:
questions.explanation: The moment arm is zero, so τ = 0 (e.g. pushing a door at its hinge).

questions.q: By convention, anticlockwise moment is taken as ______ and clockwise moment as ______.
questions.explanation: Anticlockwise (+), clockwise (−).

questions.q: A long-handled wrench is used to open a tight nut because it:
options: reduces the force on the nut
increases the moment arm, giving more torque for the same force
questions.explanation: Torque increases with moment arm.

questions.q: The axis of rotation of a door is at its:
questions.explanation: The door rotates about the line through its hinges.

questions.q: Torque plays the same role in rotational motion as ______ plays in translational motion.
questions.explanation: Net torque changes rotation just as net force changes linear motion.

questions.q: A body is in equilibrium when:
options: net force and net torque on it are both zero
questions.explanation: All forces and torques must be balanced.

questions.q: The first condition of equilibrium is:
questions.explanation: The vector sum of all forces must be zero (force polygon closes).

questions.q: The second condition of equilibrium is:
questions.explanation: The vector sum of all torques must be zero.

questions.q: The second condition of equilibrium is also called the:
questions.explanation: Sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments.

questions.q: A 4 N weight is 0.2 m from the pivot on one side of a metre rule. To balance it, a 2 N weight must be placed on the other side at:
Kamil (250 N) sits 0.6 m from a seesaw pivot. Bilal (200 N) must sit at what distance to balance?
To balance a heavier weight, a lighter weight should be placed:
questions.explanation: A larger moment arm compensates a smaller force.

questions.q: A book resting on a table is in:
questions.explanation: At rest with balanced forces (weight and normal force).

questions.q: A paratrooper falling with constant velocity is in:
questions.explanation: Moving with uniform linear velocity, net force zero.

questions.q: A ceiling fan rotating with unchanging speed is in:
questions.explanation: Uniform rotation means net torque is zero.

questions.q: A body in equilibrium must NOT have:
questions.explanation: Net force zero ⇒ acceleration zero; it may still move uniformly.

questions.q: In an experiment to verify the principle of moments with a metre rule, the rule is first balanced at its:
questions.explanation: Pivoting at its CG makes the rule's own weight produce no moment.

quizzes.topic: Centre of Mass and Centre of Gravity

questions.q: The point about which the mass of a rigid body is equally distributed is its:
questions.explanation: The CM can be treated as the point where all mass is concentrated.

questions.q: The point where the whole weight of a body appears to act is its:
questions.explanation: CG is where the entire force of gravity seems to act.

questions.q: For small objects, the centre of mass and centre of gravity are:
questions.explanation: g is the same throughout a small object.

questions.q: CM and CG of a very tall object (like a mountain) differ slightly because:
options: weight is zero at the top
questions.explanation: Slightly different g at different heights shifts the CG.

questions.q: The centre of gravity of a uniform sphere or cube lies at its:
questions.explanation: For symmetric, homogeneous objects it is the geometric centre.

questions.q: The centre of gravity of a uniform metre rod is at:
questions.explanation: So a uniform rod balances at its centre.

questions.q: The CG of an irregular plane sheet is found by suspending it from different points and using a:
questions.explanation: Vertical lines through the suspension points meet at the CG.

questions.q: The point where the plumb lines drawn from different suspension points intersect is the:
questions.explanation: The CG always lies vertically below the point of suspension.

questions.q: The centre of gravity of a ring or a bent arm can lie:
options: outside the material of the body
questions.explanation: CG may lie in empty space, e.g. centre of a ring.

questions.q: When a hammer is thrown, its centre of mass follows a:
questions.explanation: Other points rotate around the CM in complicated paths.

questions.q: If the line of action of a force passes through the centre of mass of a free body, the force:
questions.explanation: There is no moment arm about the CM, so only translation occurs.

questions.q: Stability is the ability of an object to:
options: return to its original position when the disturbing force is removed
questions.explanation: Stable objects are difficult to topple.

questions.q: A body that returns to its original position after being slightly tilted is in:
questions.explanation: E.g. a book lying flat on a table.

questions.q: In stable equilibrium, when the body is displaced its centre of mass:
questions.explanation: The weight then produces a moment that restores it.

questions.q: A pencil balanced on its tip is in:
questions.explanation: When displaced, its CG falls and it topples.

questions.q: A ball on a horizontal floor is in:
questions.explanation: It stays in its new position; its CG neither rises nor falls.

questions.q: Stability of an object can be improved by:
options: raising its CG and narrowing its base
lowering its CG and widening its base
questions.explanation: Lower CG + larger area of support = more stable.

questions.q: Racing cars are built low and wide to:
questions.explanation: Low CG and wide base prevent toppling on turns.

questions.q: Self-righting toys (wobbling dolls) return upright because their CG is:
options: low, near the heavy rounded base
questions.explanation: The weight creates a restoring moment when tilted.

questions.q: A double-decker bus is more likely to topple when its:
options: upper deck is full and lower deck empty
questions.explanation: A heavy upper deck raises the CG, reducing stability.

questions.q: A tightrope walker carries a long horizontal pole mainly to:
options: improve stability by lowering the CG and resisting rotation
questions.explanation: The pole's mass far from the body increases resistance to tipping.

questions.q: An object topples when the vertical line through its CG:
questions.explanation: The weight then produces a toppling moment.

questions.q: Standing with legs spread apart on a moving bus improves stability because it:
questions.explanation: A wider base keeps the CG over the base for larger tilts.

quizzes.topic: Friction: Sliding, Rolling and Methods to Reduce

questions.q: Friction always acts:
options: opposite to motion or attempted motion
questions.explanation: It resists relative motion between surfaces.

questions.q: The main cause of friction is:
options: interlocking of microscopic roughness of surfaces
questions.explanation: Even polished surfaces are rough under a microscope.

questions.q: Friction between brake pads and a bicycle rim is:
questions.explanation: The pads slide against the rim to slow the wheel.

questions.q: For the same weight, rolling friction is:
questions.explanation: It can be 2–3 orders of magnitude smaller.

questions.q: The invention of the wheel was a milestone because it replaced:
questions.explanation: Rolling makes moving heavy loads much easier.

questions.q: Ball bearings reduce friction by:
options: converting sliding friction into rolling friction
questions.explanation: Balls roll between moving parts.

questions.q: Applying oil or grease between machine parts reduces friction because:
options: liquids have less friction than solid surfaces in contact
questions.explanation: Lubricants separate the solid surfaces.

questions.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of friction?
options: it helps us walk without slipping
questions.explanation: Friction between shoes and ground lets us walk.

questions.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of friction?
questions.explanation: Energy is wasted as heat to overcome friction.

questions.q: It is difficult to walk on a slippery floor because of:
questions.explanation: Less friction means less grip for pushing backward.

questions.q: According to the book, wider tyres do not increase friction because friction:
options: does not depend on the area of contact
questions.explanation: Wide tyres only spread the weight, reducing heat and wear.

questions.q: Treads on tyres are mainly made to:
options: displace water from the road to avoid skidding
questions.explanation: Racing cars on dry days often use treadless tyres.

quizzes.topic: Fluid Friction, Terminal Velocity and Frictional Dissipation

questions.q: The retarding force experienced by an object moving through a fluid is called:
questions.explanation: Drag is the result of fluid friction.

questions.q: Drag force does NOT depend on the:
options: size and shape of the object
questions.explanation: It depends on size, shape, orientation, fluid and speed.

questions.q: As a falling object's speed increases, the air resistance on it:
questions.explanation: Drag increases with speed.

questions.q: Terminal velocity is reached when:
options: drag force becomes equal to weight
questions.explanation: Net force becomes zero (dynamic equilibrium).

questions.q: At terminal velocity, the acceleration of a falling body is:
questions.explanation: Speed stays constant, so acceleration is zero.

questions.q: The terminal speed of a human skydiver in air (without parachute) is about:
questions.explanation: About 53 m/s or 190 km/h.

questions.q: After the parachute opens, the terminal speed reduces to about:
questions.explanation: The large area increases drag, giving a new lower terminal velocity.

questions.q: The correct order of terminal speeds is:
questions.explanation: Heavy, compact hailstones fall fastest; light, wide snowflakes slowest.

questions.q: A force that decreases the mechanical energy of a system (converting it to heat) is called:
questions.explanation: Friction and air resistance are dissipative.

questions.q: Our hands get warm when we rub them together because of:
questions.explanation: Work against friction appears as heat.

questions.q: Shooting stars (meteors) glow because:
options: air friction/compression heats them as they plough through the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Intense heating vaporises most meteors.

questions.q: Skydivers change their body orientation to:
options: manipulate drag and control speed and direction
questions.explanation: Changing effective size and orientation changes drag.

questions.q: Motion in a circular path with constant speed is called:
questions.explanation: Speed is constant but direction changes continuously.

questions.q: In uniform circular motion, the velocity of the object:
questions.explanation: So the object is accelerating.

questions.q: The acceleration in uniform circular motion is directed:
options: towards the centre of the circle
questions.explanation: It is called centripetal (centre-seeking) acceleration.

questions.q: The force that pulls an object out of a straight-line path into a circular path is:
questions.explanation: Centripetal force acts towards the centre.

questions.q: The magnitude of centripetal force is:
questions.explanation: F_c = m v² / r.

questions.q: A 5 kg hammer ball is swung at 25 m/s on a 1.5 m wire. The centripetal force is about:
For a ball whirled on a string, the centripetal force is provided by:
questions.explanation: The string pulls the ball towards the centre.

questions.q: The centripetal force that keeps planets in orbit around the Sun is:
questions.explanation: The Sun's gravity pulls the planets towards it.

questions.q: For a car turning on a flat road, the centripetal force is provided by:
questions.explanation: If friction is insufficient the car skids outward.

questions.q: A car taking a turn too fast skids off the road due to:
questions.explanation: Required mv²/r exceeds available friction.

questions.q: If the string of a whirling stone breaks, the stone moves:
options: along the tangent in a straight line
questions.explanation: With no centripetal force it continues straight due to inertia.

questions.q: If the speed of a body in a circle is doubled (same mass and radius), the centripetal force becomes:
questions.explanation: F ∝ v², so 2² = 4 times.

questions.q: An object that orbits another object in space is called a:
questions.explanation: Satellites can be natural (Moon) or artificial (ISS).

questions.q: The time taken by an object to complete one orbit is called its:
questions.explanation: Earth's orbital period around the Sun is 365 days.

questions.q: The average orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit is:
questions.explanation: Distance in one orbit = circumference 2πr, time = T.

questions.q: Earth orbits the Sun at r = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m with T ≈ 3.16 × 10⁷ s. Its orbital speed is about:
We do not feel Earth's huge orbital speed because:
options: we move along with the Earth (relatively at rest)
questions.explanation: Motion is relative; everything around us moves with us.

questions.q: The farther a planet is from the Sun, its orbital period is:
questions.explanation: E.g. Neptune takes almost 165 years.

questions.q: The farther a planet is from the Sun, its average orbital speed is generally:
questions.explanation: Outer planets move more slowly in their orbits.

questions.q: If an artificial satellite is given too little speed at its orbit height, it will:
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls it down.

questions.q: If a satellite's speed is too high, it will:
options: move in an elliptical orbit or escape
questions.explanation: Speed must be adjusted for a circular orbit.

questions.q: A satellite's orbital speed at a given height depends on:
options: the orbit radius (not the satellite's mass)
questions.explanation: All satellites at the same height have the same speed.

questions.q: The planet with the shortest orbital period in our solar system is:
questions.explanation: Mercury is closest to the Sun (about 88 days).

questions.q: A satellite moves in a circle of radius 7000 km with period 5800 s. Its orbital speed is about:
A seesaw balances perfectly with two children of equal weight sitting at equal distances from the fulcrum. If one child moves closer to the fulcrum:
options: The seesaw tips towards the child who moved closer
The seesaw tips towards the child who stayed further away
questions.explanation: The moved child's moment decreases, so the farther child's larger moment tips the seesaw his way.

questions.q: When line of action of the applied force passes through its pivot point then moment of force acting on the body is:
questions.explanation: Moment arm is zero, so τ = F × 0 = 0.

questions.q: If a body is at rest or moving with uniform rotational velocity, then torque acting on the body will be:
questions.explanation: No change in rotation means net torque is zero.

questions.q: A body in equilibrium must not have:
questions.explanation: Net force zero ⇒ no acceleration.

questions.q: A uniformly rotating fan is said to be in:
questions.explanation: It rotates uniformly — dynamic (rotational) equilibrium.

questions.q: You throw a weighted fishing net into a calm lake. As the net sinks, it opens fully underwater. Compared to the moment it left your hand, where is the net's centre of mass now?
options: At the same depth but slightly shifted horizontally
Unchanged from its position when thrown
questions.explanation: The whole net has sunk, so its centre of mass is lower.

questions.q: A tightrope walker carries a long pole while walking across a rope. The stability of the walker is best improved if the pole is:
questions.explanation: A long horizontal pole spreads mass far from the body and resists tipping.

questions.q: It is more difficult to walk on a slippery surface than on a non-slippery one because of:
questions.explanation: Less friction means less grip.

questions.q: For an object moving with terminal velocity, its acceleration:
questions.explanation: Velocity is constant, so acceleration is zero.

questions.q: The correct order of comparison for the terminal speeds of a raindrop, snowflake and hailstone is:
questions.explanation: Heavier compact bodies have higher terminal speed.

questions.q: You are trying to loosen a nut using a spanner, but it is not working. In order to open the nut, you need to:
options: insert a pipe to increase length of spanner
use a spanner of small length
questions.explanation: Longer moment arm gives more torque.

questions.q: The force that always changes direction of velocity and not its magnitude is called:
questions.explanation: Centripetal force is perpendicular to velocity.

questions.q: The reason that a car moving on a horizontal road gets thrown out of the road while taking a turn is:
options: rolling friction between tyre and road
questions.explanation: Friction cannot supply the required mv²/r.

questions.q: A car drives at steady speed around a perfectly circular track.
options: The net force on the car is zero
Both the acceleration and net force on the car point outward
Both the acceleration and net force on the car point inward
questions.explanation: Centripetal acceleration and force point towards the centre.

questions.q: A satellite of mass m is revolving around the Earth with an orbital speed v. If mass of the satellite is doubled, its orbital speed will become:
questions.explanation: Orbital speed does not depend on the satellite's mass.
